newsitem.title: USA: Bad weather could delay U.S. Mars probe launch.
newsitem.headline: Bad weather could delay U.S. Mars probe launch.

text.p: Stormy weather was threatening the Monday launch of a NASA Mars probe carrying a small rover to explore the planet's rocky surface, NASA officials said on Saturday.
Meterologists were giving the Delta 2 rocket carrying the Mars Pathfinder probe a 1-in-10 chance of making it off the launch pad early on Monday morning.
"As far as the launch is concerned, we are going to have a lot of problems," Joel Tumbiolo, a U.S. Air Force weather officer, said.
A cold front passing through central Florida will bring thick clouds, gusty winds, rain and thunderstorms to the Cape Canaveral area during the 2:09 a.m. EST (0709 GMT) launch time, he said.

NASA managers planned to meet at 8 a.m. EST (1300 GMT) on Sunday to decide whether to proceed with the countdown or reschedule the blastoff for Tuesday morning when conditions were forecast to be near-perfect.
The Mars Pathfinder will follow NASA's Global Surveyor spacecraft on the road to the Red Planet. It will overtake the Global Surveyor, launched Nov. 7, and arrive at Mars on July 4, 1997.
The probe is to plunge through the planet's thin atmosphere, slow by parachute and bounce to a safe landing, protected by giant air bags.

The Pathfinder's pyramid-shaped lander carries a six-wheeled rover, the size of an office laser printer, called Sojourner. Under remote control from earth it will explore the landing site, beaming back pictures of the surface and sniffing out the composition of rocks.

Following the loss of Russia's Mars 96 probe and its four radioactive batteries, NASA officials were quick to stress that the one-third ounce (8 grams) of plutonium on the Pathfinder spacecraft posed little threat in the event of a launch accident.
"There was a lot on anaylsis that went on," said Don Ketterer of NASA Headquarters. "There was no credible accident which would release any plutonium."
The Sojourner rover uses three radioactive heaters, each about the size of a marshmallow, to keep the rover's axles warm in the frigid Martian climate.
